Main distribution
Ubuntu 24.04, with RHEL's SELinux in 18.8

At Stagedoor

The security assessment from Chapter 15 had nine findings. The firewall and SSH fixed the two biggest. On Thursday 29 October 2026 Rafaela sits down with the other seven: the app could write anywhere a root process can (it no longer ran as root, but nothing else restricted it); unneeded packages and services on every server; needrestart listing services still running old libraries; no record of who changed files in /etc; and, the one that worries her most, no written description of what a correctly set-up server is. Each server had been fixed by hand, carefully, and slightly differently.

The new server Stagedoor needs next, a replacement for door-2 (whose Ubuntu 22.04 support ends in April), is the chance to write that description down and build from it.

18.1What hardening is for

Hardening assumes something will eventually go wrong (an unpatched bug in the app, a stolen laptop with a key on it, a mistake in a firewall rule) and arranges the server so that one failure doesn't become everything.

Three principles run through every layer: least function (don't run, install or expose what you don't need), least privilege (give each thing only the access its job requires, Handbook 2, Chapter 6), and verify, don't assume (measure the result, and keep checking it).

18.2Attack surface: what's there to attack?

Start with an inventory, using commands from earlier chapters:

Table 18.1 · An attack-surface inventory
QuestionCommandReduce it by
What listens on the network?sudo ss -tlnp, sudo ss -ulnpstopping services, binding to 127.0.0.1, firewall rules
What starts at boot?systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabledsystemctl disable --now, removing packages
What runs with root's power?ps -eo user,comm | awk '$1=="root"' | sort -uservices as their own users
Which programs are setuid?sudo find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type fremoving packages that bring unneeded ones
Who can log in, and with what?getent passwd, authorized_keys audit (Chapter 16)removing accounts and keys
Who can become root?getent group sudo, /etc/sudoers.d/narrow rules (Chapter 4)
What's installed?apt list --installed | wc -lminimal images; removing what isn't needed

Every item on the list is something that could have a vulnerability, a misconfiguration or a forgotten credential. The cheapest hardening is removal: a service that doesn't run can't be exploited, and a package that isn't installed doesn't need patching. Cloud images help by starting small; “minimal” images start smaller still.

18.3Sandboxing services with systemd

A service running as its own user (Chapter 4) can't read other users' files, but it can still read most of the system, write wherever that user may, see devices, load code into memory as it likes, and make any system call. If an attacker gets code execution in the app, all of that is theirs. systemd can remove most of it before the process starts (Chapter 6 previewed this):

hardening.confsystemd drop-in

# /etc/systemd/system/stagedoor.service.d/hardening.conf · take away what the app doesn't need
# (systemd allows comments only on lines of their own, never after a setting)
[Service]
# no setuid programs, no gaining privileges, and no root powers at all
NoNewPrivileges=yes
CapabilityBoundingSet=
# the whole filesystem read-only, except the app's own data
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/stagedoor
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
# no devices, no changes to the kernel, its logs, the clock or the hostname
PrivateDevices=yes
ProtectKernelTunables=yes
ProtectKernelModules=yes
ProtectKernelLogs=yes
ProtectControlGroups=yes
ProtectClock=yes
ProtectHostname=yes
RestrictNamespaces=yes
RestrictRealtime=yes
RestrictSUIDSGID=yes
LockPersonality=yes
# only IP and local sockets, only the system calls a normal service makes
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX
SystemCallArchitectures=native
SystemCallFilter=@system-service
SystemCallFilter=~@privileged @resources
  • Filesystem: ProtectSystem=strict mounts everything read-only for this service, ReadWritePaths= opens exactly the paths it writes, ProtectHome hides home directories, PrivateTmp gives it an empty /tmp of its own.
  • Privileges: NoNewPrivileges blocks setuid programs (so sudo or su are useless from inside), and an empty CapabilityBoundingSet removes every root capability, even if the process somehow became root.
  • Kernel and devices: no hardware devices, no changing kernel settings, modules, logs, the clock or the hostname.
  • System calls: SystemCallFilter=@system-service allows the calls a normal service makes and refuses the rest (mounting, rebooting, loading kernel modules, tracing other processes); RestrictAddressFamilies allows only IP and local sockets.

systemd-analyze security scores a unit's exposure from 0 (locked down) to 10 (nothing restricted) and lists each missing setting. In the lab, Stagedoor's app goes from 9.2 to 1.5 with this drop-in, and still works. Add settings in small groups and test the app after each: a service that writes somewhere you forgot fails with “Read-only file system”, and one that needs a refused system call is killed with SIGSYS, both of which the journal records.

Key idea

Assume the app will one day run an attacker's code. Decide now what that code may touch, and let systemd enforce it.

18.4An audit trail

Logs (Chapter 7) record what programs say. An audit trail records what happened, from the kernel's point of view, whether or not any program mentions it: who changed /etc/sudoers, who ran a command as root, which process opened a sensitive file. On Linux this is the kernel's audit system, configured with auditd (sudo apt install auditd):

# writes or attribute changes to sudoers and the SSH configuration, tagged for searching
-w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k sudoers
-w /etc/sudoers.d/ -p wa -k sudoers
-w /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ -p wa -k sshd
# commands run as root by a real person (audit UID 1000 and up)
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -F euid=0 -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -k root-commands

Rules like these go in /etc/audit/rules.d/; sudo ausearch -k sudoers -i finds the events, each with the audit UID: the person who logged in, which stays the same through sudo and su. That's the accountability question from Handbook 2, Chapter 1, answered at the level of the kernel. The audit trail is only useful if it survives an attacker: ship it off the server with the other logs. (The test system for this book is a container, where the kernel's audit system isn't available, so these rules are shown, not run.)

18.5A baseline: written, built and checked

A baseline is the written description of a correctly set-up server, the thing Stagedoor lacked. It works only if it's written in a form that can be applied and checked, not just read. For Stagedoor's web servers, collected from this book:

Table 18.2 · Stagedoor's server baseline, and where each item comes from
AreaBaselineChapter
Releasean Ubuntu LTS with at least a year of support left1, 8
Accountspersonal accounts in sudo and ssh-users; no shared accounts; root locked4
SSHkeys only, no root, AllowGroups ssh-users, LogLevel VERBOSE16
Firewallnftables default deny, per-role file from Git15
Updatesunattended security updates; weekly restart and reboot window8
Servicesown users, UMask=0027, sandbox drop-ins, limits6, 12, 18
Logsjournal capped, logrotate for files, shipped off the server7
Disksdata on its own volume; space and inode alerts11
Auditauditd rules for privilege and configuration changes18
Nothing elseno unneeded packages, services or listening ports18

Then make it executable in two forms. A first-boot configuration in cloud-init (Chapter 1) builds the parts that belong to every server; the lab validates one with cloud-init schema, which catches typos and wrong types before a server boots with them. And a build script does the rest and can check itself, which is Chapter 21's capstone. Configuration-management tools (Ansible, Salt, Puppet) are the grown-up version of both: the same idea, with modules that are idempotent by design.

18.6Benchmarks and scanners

You don't have to invent a baseline from nothing. The CIS Benchmarks are detailed, versioned hardening guides per distribution, with hundreds of checks in two levels (Level 1: sensible for most servers; Level 2: stricter, may break things). Ubuntu Pro's Ubuntu Security Guide (usg) can apply and audit them automatically; OpenSCAP does the same for RHEL. Lynis, a free scanner, runs a few hundred checks and prints suggestions and a “hardening index” from 0 to 100.

Use them as a second opinion, not a goal. A score measures how many boxes are ticked, not whether the server is safe for what it does: some suggestions don't apply (a web server needs its web port open), some cost more than they're worth, and the most important controls in this book (no shared accounts, no long-lived keys, patches actually running) are things a scanner can only partly see. Read the suggestions, apply what fits, write down why you skipped the rest, and track the score over time so that it doesn't quietly fall.

18.7A few kernel settings

A handful of sysctl settings (Chapter 12) are worth including in a baseline. Ubuntu already sets several; check each with sysctl before adding it:

# hide kernel addresses, and the kernel log, from unprivileged users
kernel.kptr_restrict = 2
kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1
# no BPF programs for ordinary users
kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled = 1
# drop packets with impossible source addresses; ignore ICMP redirects
net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0
# the /tmp symlink tricks from Chapter 17's warning
fs.protected_symlinks = 1

18.8Across distributions: AppArmor and SELinux

Both families add a second, mandatory access-control layer on top of permissions (Chapter 4): a policy, set by the administrator, that even a process running as root can't override. They do with policy files what this chapter's systemd settings do per service.

AppArmor (Ubuntu, Debian) and SELinux (RHEL family, Amazon Linux)

AppArmor confines programs by path: a profile lists the files and capabilities a program may use. Ubuntu ships profiles for several services; sudo aa-status lists them, and denials appear in the journal as apparmor="DENIED". SELinux labels every file and process with a context and allows interactions by rules between labels (Chapter 3 and Chapter 4's boxes). It's on in enforcing mode by default on RHEL; getenforce shows the mode, sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent the denials, and restorecon fixes labels on moved files. The common mistake on both is switching them off at the first denial: read the denial, then fix the label or the profile.

At Stagedoor: a baseline in three forms

By the end of the week, Table 18.2 is in the operations repository three times: as a checklist anyone can read, as baseline.yaml for first boots (checked with cloud-init schema in CI, next to ShellCheck), and as the beginning of a build script. stagedoor.service and the payouts timer get sandbox drop-ins; the app's score goes from 9.2 to 1.5, nginx's from 9.6 to 4.1 once its writable paths are listed. auditd records changes to sudoers, the SSH configuration and the firewall, and commands run as root by people, and its log ships with the rest. Unneeded packages go (a leftover FTP server on door-3 among them).

Lynis on door-2 scores 58 before and 81 after; Rafaela writes the score into the wiki with a date, and a reason next to each suggestion left open. The retest on 15 October had already closed the network findings; the assessment firm closes the remaining seven on 12 November. And Tiago starts the script that will build door-5, door-2's replacement, from the baseline (Chapter 21).

18.10Common mistakes

MistakeWhat happensInstead
Hardening by hand, server by serverEach server slightly different; nobody knows the intended state.A written baseline, applied by cloud-init and scripts, checked regularly.
Chasing a scanner's scoreBoxes ticked, real risks (shared accounts, old keys) untouched.Use scores as a second opinion; decide per suggestion.
Applying every sandbox setting at onceThe service breaks and the whole drop-in is reverted.Small groups, test after each, read the journal.
Disabling AppArmor or SELinux at the first denialThe whole mandatory layer is gone, for one mislabelled file.Read the denial; fix the label or profile.
Audit logs only on the serverThe intruder deletes them.Ship them off immediately.
Never validating first-boot configurationTypos are ignored silently; servers boot half-configured.cloud-init schema in CI.

✓Chapter summary

  • Hardening limits what one failure can lead to: layers from the network to the data, each assuming the outer one might fail.
  • Start with the attack surface: listening services, enabled units, root processes, setuid programs, accounts and keys. Remove what isn't needed.
  • systemd sandboxing (ProtectSystem, NoNewPrivileges, capabilities, system-call filters) limits a compromised service; systemd-analyze security measures it.
  • An audit trail (auditd) records privileged actions and changes by the person who logged in; ship it off the server.
  • Write a baseline and make it executable (cloud-init, scripts) and checkable; use CIS, Lynis and similar as second opinions.
  • AppArmor (Ubuntu) and SELinux (RHEL) add mandatory access control; fix denials, don't disable the layer.

Key terms

Hardening
Reducing a system's attack surface and the privileges of what runs on it, so a single failure does less damage.
Attack surface
Everything an attacker could try to use: listening services, accounts, credentials, privileged programs, installed software.
Sandboxing
Restricting what a process may access (files, devices, system calls, privileges) beyond ordinary permissions.
Capability
One of the separate privileges into which Linux divides root's power, such as binding low ports or overriding file permissions.
Audit trail
A record of security-relevant actions from the kernel's point of view, tied to the person who logged in.
Baseline
The written, checkable description of a correctly configured server.
Mandatory access control
Access rules set by policy that processes, even root ones, can't override; AppArmor and SELinux on Linux.

Check your understanding

  1. Name four things to list when measuring a server's attack surface, and a command for each. recall

    Show answer

    Listening sockets (sudo ss -tlnp), enabled services (systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled), setuid programs (sudo find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f), accounts and keys that can log in (getent passwd plus the authorized_keys audit); also sudo rules and installed packages.

  2. A payouts timer writes its CSV to /var/lib/stagedoor/payouts/ and reads /etc/stagedoor/stagedoor.env. Write the filesystem part of its sandbox. apply

    Show answer

    ProtectSystem=strict, ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/stagedoor/payouts, ProtectHome=yes, PrivateTmp=yes. Reading /etc/stagedoor needs nothing extra (strict makes it read-only, not invisible); the file permissions still decide whether the service's user may read it.

  3. Explain why NoNewPrivileges=yes matters even for a service that never runs sudo. explain

    Show answer

    It's about what an attacker could do with the service's process, not what the service does. Without it, code running in the service could run a setuid program (sudo, su, a vulnerable helper) and gain privileges; with it, setuid bits and file capabilities are ignored for that process and its children.

  4. After you add a sandbox drop-in, a service starts but its file uploads fail with “Read-only file system”, and another service dies with signal SYS. What happened in each case, and how do you fix them? debug

    Show answer

    The first writes to a path not in ReadWritePaths= under ProtectSystem=strict: find the path in the error and add it (or use StateDirectory=/CacheDirectory=). The second made a system call outside SystemCallFilter=: the journal or journalctl -k names it; allow that group (or call), or reconsider whether the service should be making it.

  5. Design how Stagedoor keeps four servers matching its baseline over a year. design

    Show answer

    The baseline lives in Git as a checklist, cloud-init and a build script, all reviewed. New servers are built from it, never by hand. A scheduled check (the build script in verify mode, plus Lynis, systemd-analyze security scores and the SSH and sudo audits) runs weekly and reports differences. Fixes go into the baseline first, then onto servers, ideally by rebuilding. Scores and decisions are dated in the wiki.

  6. Compare systemd sandboxing with AppArmor for confining the app. compare

    Show answer

    systemd's settings are per unit, short and readable, apply to everything the service starts, and need no extra framework; they can't express fine-grained per-file rules as easily. An AppArmor profile is per program, can list exactly which files it may read and write, and applies however the program is started, but profiles take more effort to write and maintain. Using both is possible; for your own services, systemd's sandbox is the easier first step.

Going further

  • man systemd.exec (the sandboxing sections) and systemd-analyze security --help.
  • CIS Benchmarks and Canonical's Ubuntu Security Guide.
  • Lynis and man auditd, man audit.rules, man ausearch.
  • cloud-init: module reference and the schema command.

Part V · Automation and security

19

Containers are Linux

A container isn't a small virtual machine. It's an ordinary Linux process that the kernel shows a different view of the system: its own process numbers, its own network, its own root filesystem, and limits on what it may use. This chapter builds one by hand from the pieces you already know, then shows what that means for the containers you'll run: why PID 1 matters, where image layers come from, and how isolated a container really is.

By the end you can

  • Explain a container as namespaces, cgroups and a root filesystem, and build one with unshare.
  • Explain image layers with overlayfs, including how deletions work.
  • Write a container entrypoint that receives signals and doesn't leave zombies.
  • Find a container's process, limits and kernel messages from the host.
  • Compare containers and VMs for isolation, and choose between them.

Before you start

  • Chapter 5 (PID 1, signals, zombies), Chapter 10 (cgroups, OOM), Chapter 13 (network namespaces).
  • A Linux VM with sudo and Docker (sudo apt install docker.io) (Appendix C).

This chapter

Reading
about 45 minutes
Lab
35 minutes, a Linux VM with Docker, free
Main distribution
any; containers are the kernel's

At Stagedoor

In November 2026, Sasha's team packages the app as a container image, first for developers' laptops and then, eventually, for the cloud (Handbooks 4 and 5). On Thursday 5 November, Tiago runs a load test against his first image and finds two problems. Stopping the container always takes exactly ten seconds and kills the checkouts in progress, although the app handles SIGTERM gracefully (Chapter 5). And after the test, the container holds four thousand zombie processes, left by the helper that renders PDF tickets.

The same week Leonor asks a question that sounds simple: if each service runs in its own container, are they as separate as if each had its own server? Could the payment service share a machine with everything else?

19.1A container is a process

Run ps on a machine with containers and you'll find their programs in the list, next to everything else, because that's what they are: processes, started by the container runtime, running on the host's kernel. What makes them “containers” is three kernel features applied to them:

  • Namespaces change what a process can see: its own process IDs, mounts, network stack, hostname and users.
  • cgroups change what it can use: CPU, memory, number of processes, I/O (Chapters 9 and 10).
  • A root filesystem of its own, usually assembled from image layers by overlayfs, so it sees a whole distribution's files without a disk of its own.

Add security settings (dropped capabilities, a system-call filter, an AppArmor or SELinux profile: Chapter 18's list) and that's a container. Docker, Podman, containerd and Kubernetes all assemble the same kernel pieces.

19.2Namespaces

Table 19.1 · Linux namespaces
NamespaceGives the process its own…unshare option
PIDprocess numbers: the first process inside is PID 1--pid --fork
Mountlist of mounts, and so its own root filesystem--mount, --root
Networkinterfaces, addresses, routes, firewall, sockets (Chapter 13)--net
UTShostname--uts
IPCshared-memory segments and message queues--ipc
Useruser IDs: root inside can be an ordinary user outside (“rootless”)--user
Cgroup, timeview of the cgroup tree; clock offsets--cgroup, --time

Every process has a namespace of each type; ls -l /proc/<pid>/ns/ shows which, and two processes in the same container point to the same ones. unshare starts a program in new namespaces; nsenter runs a program inside an existing process's namespaces, which is what docker exec does, and a handy debugging trick: sudo nsenter -t <pid> -n ss -tlnp lists a container's listening sockets with the host's tools.

19.3cgroups: the limits

A container's limits are cgroup files (Chapter 10). docker run --memory 64m writes 64 MB into the memory controller's limit for the container's cgroup; --cpus 0.5 sets a CPU quota, --pids-limit caps the number of processes. When a container goes over its memory limit, the kernel's OOM killer acts inside that cgroup only, exactly as in Lab 10, and the container exits with 137. From the host, cat /proc/<pid>/cgroup shows a process's cgroup path, and the files under /sys/fs/cgroup/ show its limits and usage.

There are two versions of the cgroup interface. cgroup v2, one unified tree with files like memory.max, is the default on Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 11+, RHEL 9 and Amazon Linux 2023. Older systems (and this book's test machine) use v1, with a tree per controller and files like memory.limit_in_bytes. Same idea, different file names.

19.4Images and layers

A container image is a stack of read-only layers, each a set of files produced by one step of the build (a COPY, a RUN apt-get install), plus metadata such as the command to run. When a container starts, the runtime stacks the layers with overlayfs and adds one writable layer on top:

Two practical consequences. Deleting a file in a later build step doesn't shrink the image (the earlier layer still contains it, hidden by a whiteout), which is why Dockerfiles install and clean up in one RUN, and why a secret copied into an early layer stays in the image even if a later step deletes it. And data a container must keep (uploads, a database) goes on a volume, a directory mounted from outside the overlay.

19.5PID 1 in a container

The first process in a PID namespace is PID 1 there, and the kernel treats PID 1 specially (Chapter 5):

  • No default signal actions. A signal that PID 1 hasn't installed a handler for is ignored, even SIGTERM. A program that would normally die on SIGTERM does nothing as PID 1; the runtime waits its stop timeout (10 seconds for docker stop, 30 for Kubernetes by default) and sends SIGKILL: exit status 137, requests in flight lost.
  • Orphans are adopted by PID 1, which must reap them. An application never written to be an init system doesn't, and finished orphans pile up as zombies.

Three habits fix both:

  1. Exec form in the Dockerfile: CMD ["python3", "/app/checkout.py"], not CMD python3 /app/checkout.py. The shell form runs /bin/sh -c "…", so PID 1 is a shell that neither forwards signals nor exits; the exec form makes your program PID 1. In an entrypoint script, end with exec "$@" (Chapter 5).
  2. Handle SIGTERM in the program: as PID 1 it's the only way it reacts at all.
  3. A tiny init as PID 1 when the program starts children: docker run --init (or tini in the image) runs a minimal init that forwards signals to your program and reaps orphans.

Key idea

In a container, your program is PID 1. Make it the program (exec form), make it handle SIGTERM, and give it an init if it has children.

19.6How isolated is a container?

All containers on a host share its kernel, so the kernel's system-call interface, hundreds of calls wide, is the boundary between them. A kernel vulnerability, a container run with --privileged, or a sensitive host path mounted in (the Docker socket, /) can let a process escape to the host. A VM's boundary is narrower: a hypervisor emulating a handful of virtual devices. That difference is the answer to “are containers as separate as servers?”: they're good isolation between cooperating workloads you trust roughly equally, and weaker isolation between strangers.

Between the two sit sandboxed runtimes: gVisor answers system calls in a user-space kernel; Kata Containers and Firecracker run each container or function in a lightweight VM. AWS Lambda and Fargate use Firecracker, and so, as Lab 1 noticed, did the machine this book was tested on. Whatever the runtime, the hardening from Chapter 18 applies inside: run as a non-root user, drop capabilities, read-only root filesystem, no --privileged.

19.7Across distributions

On the RHEL family

RHEL ships Podman instead of Docker: the same command-line options and image format, no central daemon, and rootless containers by default, using user namespaces so that root in the container is your own user on the host. It can also generate systemd units for containers (Quadlet), tying this chapter to Chapter 6. Ubuntu packages both Docker (docker.io) and Podman. Kubernetes uses containerd or CRI-O directly; Handbook 4 picks up from here.

19.8Lab: a container by hand, then by Docker

Lab 19 · Namespaces, layers, PID 1

You'll try namespaces one at a time, build a container from an exported image and unshare, see overlayfs and a whiteout, then reproduce Tiago's two problems with Docker and fix them, and find a container's cgroup from the host. You need a Linux VM with sudo and Docker, and Lab 5's checkout.py. Cost: nothing (the images are about 300 MB). Clean-up: the last step. PIDs, IDs and times will differ.

  1. One namespace at a time. A PID namespace (the first process is PID 1), a UTS namespace (a hostname of its own), a network namespace (nothing but a loopback, down): 
    sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc ps -ef
    UID          PID    PPID  C STIME TTY          TIME CMD
root           1       0  0 12:25 ?        00:00:00 ps -ef
    hostname; sudo unshare --uts sh -c 'hostname minibox; hostname'; hostname
    vm
minibox
vm
    sudo unshare --net ip -br address
    lo               DOWN
  2. A root filesystem. Export Ubuntu's container image into a directory (any other source of a root filesystem works, such as the Ubuntu Base tarball from cdimage.ubuntu.com): 
    mkdir -p ~/lab19 && cd ~/lab19
sudo docker create --name rootfs-src ubuntu:24.04
mkdir rootfs && sudo docker export rootfs-src | sudo tar -x -C rootfs && sudo docker rm rootfs-src
ls rootfs
    An ordinary-looking Linux tree, 84 MB.
  3. A container by hand. Save and run:

    minibox.shbash

    #!/usr/bin/env bash
# minibox.sh ROOTFS · a container by hand: new namespaces, another root filesystem, a shell inside
set -euo pipefail
rootfs=${1:?usage: sudo ./minibox.sh ROOTFS-DIRECTORY}

# --pid --fork: its own process numbers (the shell inside is PID 1)
# --mount, --uts, --ipc, --net: its own mounts, hostname, IPC objects and network stack
# --root: the root directory becomes ROOTFS, so it sees only that filesystem
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # the inner script is single-quoted on purpose: it must expand inside the container
exec unshare --pid --fork --mount --uts --ipc --net --root="$rootfs" /bin/bash -c '
  mount -t proc proc /proc
  hostname minibox
  echo "hostname:   $(hostname)"
  echo "os:         $(. /etc/os-release && echo "$PRETTY_NAME")"
  echo "kernel:     $(uname -r)"
  echo "interfaces: $(tail -n +3 /proc/net/dev | cut -d: -f1 | tr -d " " | tr "\n" " ")"
  echo "processes:"
  for p in /proc/[0-9]*; do echo "  PID $(basename "$p"): $(tr "\0\n" "  " < "$p/cmdline" | cut -c1-30)…"; done
'
    chmod +x minibox.sh; sudo ./minibox.sh rootfs
    hostname:   minibox
os:         Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS
kernel:     6.18.44-fc-v880
interfaces: lo 
processes:
  PID 1: /bin/bash -c    mount -t proc …
    Its own hostname, Ubuntu's files, only a loopback interface, and one process: itself, as PID 1. But kernel is the host's kernel (here, Lab 1's microVM kernel): there's only one. (Note the shellcheck disable comment: a justified exception, as Chapter 17 asked.)
  4. Layers with overlayfs. Use rootfs as a read-only lower layer, write and delete through the merged view, then look at each layer: 
    mkdir -p upper work merged
sudo mount -t overlay overlay -o lowerdir=rootfs,upperdir=upper,workdir=work merged
echo "tickets" | sudo tee merged/etc/stagedoor-note > /dev/null
sudo rm merged/etc/legal
ls upper/etc; ls -l upper/etc/legal
ls rootfs/etc/stagedoor-note rootfs/etc/legal
sudo umount merged
    legal
stagedoor-note
c--------- 2 root root 0, 0 Nov 27 12:25 upper/etc/legal
ls: cannot access 'rootfs/etc/stagedoor-note': No such file or directory
rootfs/etc/legal
    The new file is only in upper; the lower layer still has legal; the deletion is a whiteout, a character device with numbers 0, 0, that hides it in the merged view. That's every container's writable layer, and every “deleted” file in a later image layer.
  5. Tiago's first image: shell-form CMD. In ~/lab19/img, with checkout.py from Lab 5 and orphans.py (step 7), save:

    Dockerfile.shellDockerfile

    FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY checkout.py /app/checkout.py
CMD python3 /app/checkout.py --graceful

    Dockerfile.execDockerfile

    FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY checkout.py orphans.py /app/
CMD ["python3", "/app/checkout.py", "--graceful"]
    sudo docker build -q -t lab19:shell -f Dockerfile.shell .
sudo docker build -q -t lab19:exec -f Dockerfile.exec .
sudo docker run -d --name shellform lab19:shell
sudo docker exec shellform cat /proc/1/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '; echo
time -p sudo docker stop shellform; sudo docker inspect -f 'exit code {{.State.ExitCode}}' shellform
    /bin/sh -c python3 /app/checkout.py --graceful 
shellform
real 10.14
exit code 137
    PID 1 is /bin/sh (dash, in this image), which doesn't pass SIGTERM on and, as PID 1, ignores it: ten seconds, then SIGKILL, 137.
  6. Exec form, with the graceful handler, and then without it: 
    sudo docker run -d --name execform lab19:exec
sudo docker exec execform cat /proc/1/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '; echo
time -p sudo docker stop execform; sudo docker inspect -f 'exit code {{.State.ExitCode}}' execform; sudo docker logs execform
    python3 /app/checkout.py --graceful 
execform
real 0.33
exit code 0
pid 1 listening on 127.0.0.1:8080
got SIGTERM: no new requests, finishing the ones in progress
all requests finished; exiting
    sudo docker run -d --name nohandler lab19:exec python3 /app/checkout.py
time -p sudo docker stop nohandler; sudo docker inspect -f 'exit code {{.State.ExitCode}}' nohandler
    nohandler
real 10.16
exit code 137
    With the handler: a third of a second, exit 0, the graceful messages in the log. Without it, Python as PID 1 has no default action for SIGTERM either: ten seconds and 137 again. Both fixes are needed.
  7. Orphans and zombies. Save as orphans.py (rebuild lab19:exec if you hadn't yet):

    orphans.pyPython 3.8+

    # orphans.py · run a helper that leaves a child behind, then list this container's processes
import os, subprocess, time

subprocess.run(["sh", "-c", "sleep 1 & exit 0"])   # the helper exits at once; its child "sleep" is orphaned
time.sleep(3)                                       # the orphan finishes meanwhile
for pid in sorted(int(p) for p in os.listdir("/proc") if p.isdigit()):
    fields = open(f"/proc/{pid}/stat").read().split()
    print(f"PID {pid:>3}  parent {fields[3]:>3}  state {fields[2]}  {fields[1]}")
    sudo docker run --rm lab19:exec python3 /app/orphans.py
    PID   1  parent   0  state R  (python3)
PID   8  parent   1  state Z  (sleep)
    sudo docker run --rm --init lab19:exec python3 /app/orphans.py
    PID   1  parent   0  state S  (docker-init)
PID   7  parent   1  state R  (python3)
    Without an init, the orphaned sleep was adopted by PID 1, our Python program, which never reaps: a zombie (Z). With --init, Docker's tiny init is PID 1, our program is PID 7, and the orphan was reaped as soon as it finished. Tiago's four thousand zombies were PDF helpers, one per ticket.
  8. The container from the host. Its process, cgroup and limit; then a container that goes over its limit: 
    sudo docker run -d --name memlab2 --memory 64m lab19:exec sleep 60
pid=$(sudo docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' memlab2); echo "host PID of the container's process: $pid"
grep -E ':memory:|^0::' /proc/$pid/cgroup
p=$(grep ':memory:' /proc/$pid/cgroup | cut -d: -f3); cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory$p/memory.limit_in_bytes
    host PID of the container's process: 30223
4:memory:/docker/9df89bb2c4f68887c3def899fd37a39ab21b8728ee8c500ce1bb254bfc0cfcc1
0::/docker/9df89bb2c4f68887c3def899fd37a39ab21b8728ee8c500ce1bb254bfc0cfcc1
67108864
    A process on the host like any other, in a cgroup named after the container, with a limit of 67,108,864 bytes: 64 MB. (This test machine uses cgroup v1. On cgroup v2 there's only the 0:: line, and the limit is in /sys/fs/cgroup<path>/memory.max.) Now exceed it: 
    sudo docker run --name memlab --memory 64m --memory-swap 64m lab19:exec python3 -c "x = bytearray(200 * 1024 * 1024)"
sudo docker inspect -f 'exit code {{.State.ExitCode}}, OOMKilled {{.State.OOMKilled}}' memlab
sudo dmesg | grep -i "killed process" | tail -1
    exit code 137, OOMKilled false
Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 30123 (python3) total-vm:218996kB, anon-rss:64896kB, file-rss:5708kB, shmem-rss:0kB, UID:0 pgtables:184kB oom_score_adj:0
    Exit 137 and the kernel's own record of the kill, inside the container's cgroup, yet Docker reported OOMKilled false on this test machine (its OOM detection relies on events this cgroup-v1 setup didn't deliver). On most systems it says true; when it doesn't, the kernel log is the authority (Chapter 10).
  9. Image layers, newest first: 
    sudo docker history --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}' lab19:exec | cut -c1-90 | head -6
    0B	CMD ["python3" "/app/checkout.py" "--gracefu…
16.4kB	COPY checkout.py orphans.py /app/ # buildkit
0B	CMD ["python3"]
16.4kB	RUN /bin/sh -c set -eux;  for src in idle3 p…
41.4MB	RUN /bin/sh -c set -eux;   savedAptMark="$(a…
0B	ENV PYTHON_SHA256=b5796915dc45ff745cfb4e990a…
    Each build step is a layer; our two steps are the top two (16.4 kB of files, and the CMD metadata); the rest is the Python base image, shared with every image built on it.
  10. Clean up. 
    sudo docker rm -f shellform execform nohandler memlab memlab2
sudo docker rmi lab19:shell lab19:exec

Stretch goals. (1) Give minibox.sh a network: create a veth pair, move one end into the container's namespace (ip link set … netns <pid>), and attach the other to Chapter 13's bridge. (2) Add a cgroup to minibox.sh with sudo systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=100M ./minibox.sh rootfs. (3) Run sudo nsenter -t $pid -n ip -br address against a running Docker container and compare with docker exec.

At Stagedoor: an image that stops in a third of a second

Tiago's Dockerfile switches to the exec form with --init semantics built in: the image installs tini as its entrypoint, so the app receives SIGTERM directly and the PDF helpers' orphans are reaped. docker stop now takes under a second, the load test ends with no failed checkouts, and the zombie count stays at zero. The image runs as a non-root user, with a read-only root filesystem and uploads on a volume, following Chapter 18.

Leonor's question gets a written answer: containers on one host share its kernel, so they're separated well enough for Stagedoor's own services, which trust one another roughly equally, but the payment service, which handles card data, should not share a kernel with anything it doesn't have to. When Stagedoor moves to AWS, it will get its own VMs or Fargate tasks, each in its own Firecracker micro-VM. Handbook 4 tells the Kubernetes side; Handbook 5 the infrastructure.

19.9Common mistakes

MistakeWhat happensInstead
Shell-form CMD or an entrypoint script without execSignals go to a shell; every stop is a 10-second SIGKILL.Exec form; exec "$@" at the end of scripts.
An app as PID 1 that starts childrenZombies accumulate; eventually no new processes.--init or tini.
Treating containers as VMs for isolationA kernel bug or a privileged container exposes the host.VMs or sandboxed runtimes between untrusted workloads.
--privileged, or mounting the Docker socketThe container can take over the host.Grant specific capabilities or devices only.
Secrets copied into an image layerStill in the image after a later step deletes them.Build secrets, or inject at run time.
Data written inside the container's own layerLost when the container is removed.Volumes for anything that must persist.

✓Chapter summary

  • A container is a group of ordinary processes given their own view (namespaces), limits (cgroups) and root filesystem, on the host's shared kernel.
  • unshare and nsenter create and enter namespaces; containers are built from the same pieces.
  • Images are read-only layers stacked by overlayfs under a writable layer; deletions are whiteouts; data that matters goes on volumes.
  • Your program is PID 1: no default signal actions, and it must reap orphans. Use exec form, handle SIGTERM, add an init.
  • Containers share a kernel: good isolation between trusted services, weaker than VMs between strangers. Harden them like services (Chapter 18).

Key terms

Container
A process (or group of processes) isolated with namespaces, limited with cgroups and given its own root filesystem, on a shared kernel.
Namespace
A kernel feature that gives processes their own view of one kind of system resource, such as process IDs or the network.
Container image
A stack of read-only filesystem layers plus metadata, from which containers are started.
overlayfs
A filesystem that stacks read-only lower directories under a writable upper one and presents the merged result.
Whiteout
A marker in an upper overlay layer that hides a file present in a lower layer.
Exec form
A Dockerfile CMD or ENTRYPOINT written as a JSON list, run directly rather than through /bin/sh -c.
Init process
The process running as PID 1, responsible for handling signals and reaping orphaned children.

Check your understanding

  1. Which three kernel features make a process a container? recall

    Show answer

    Namespaces (its own view of PIDs, mounts, network, hostname, IPC, users), cgroups (resource limits and accounting) and its own root filesystem (usually overlayfs layers), plus security restrictions such as dropped capabilities and system-call filters.

  2. Rewrite CMD gunicorn app:app --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 so the container stops gracefully. apply

    Show answer

    CMD ["gunicorn", "app:app", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"], so gunicorn is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM (gunicorn handles it gracefully). If it starts subprocesses that may be orphaned, add an init: ENTRYPOINT ["tini", "--"] or docker run --init.

  3. Explain why deleting a 500 MB file in a later Dockerfile step doesn't make the image smaller. explain

    Show answer

    Each step creates a new layer; the file is still in the earlier layer, and the deletion only adds a whiteout in the later one that hides it. The image contains every layer. Remove files in the same RUN step that created them, or use a multi-stage build that copies only what's needed into the final image.

  4. A container's log shows the app handling SIGTERM when you run it with docker run in the foreground and press Ctrl+C, but docker stop always takes 10 seconds. What's different? debug

    Show answer

    Ctrl+C sends SIGINT, which the app (or the shell in front of it) may handle; docker stop sends SIGTERM to PID 1. Most likely PID 1 is a shell (shell-form CMD or a wrapper script without exec) that ignores SIGTERM as PID 1 and doesn't forward it, or the app handles SIGINT but not SIGTERM. Check docker exec … cat /proc/1/cmdline.

  5. Design how Stagedoor should run the payment service and the public web app when it moves to containers. design

    Show answer

    Separate kernels for different trust levels: the payment service on its own VMs or in a sandboxed runtime (Fargate's Firecracker micro-VMs, or Kata/gVisor nodes), not on the same container hosts as public-facing services. Every container: non-root user, dropped capabilities, read-only root filesystem, resource limits, exec-form entrypoint with an init, secrets injected at run time, images scanned and pinned. Network policies between services (Handbook 4).

  6. Compare a container and a VM for running a nightly batch job from a vendor you don't fully trust. compare

    Show answer

    A container starts in a second and is cheap, but shares the host's kernel, so a kernel exploit or misconfiguration could reach other workloads. A VM costs more and starts more slowly, but its boundary is the hypervisor, much narrower than the system-call interface. For untrusted code, a VM (or a micro-VM sandbox) is the safer choice; a hardened container on a dedicated host is a middle ground.

Going further

  • man 7 namespaces, man 7 cgroups, man unshare, man nsenter; the kernel's overlayfs documentation.
  • Docker: Shell and exec form and the --init option; tini.
  • Julia Evans, How Containers Work.
  • Handbook 1, Chapter 19 (container networking) and Handbook 2, Chapter 16 (Kubernetes and workload identity).

Part VI · Running it

20

A troubleshooting method

The chapters so far each explained one thing that can go wrong. Real incidents don't arrive labelled: “the site is slow” could be any of them, or none. This chapter turns the book into a method: describe the symptom precisely, ask what changed, sweep every resource for utilisation, saturation and errors, and confirm before you act, with a script that gathers the first five minutes of facts in one go.

By the end you can

  • Turn a vague report into a precise, testable symptom.
  • Apply the USE method (utilisation, saturation, errors) to CPU, memory, disk, network and limits.
  • Collect the first five minutes of evidence on a Linux server with one script, and read it.
  • Find what changed, act with the smallest safe step, and verify.
  • Write an incident note that helps the next person.

Before you start

  • Part III (Chapters 9–12) above all; Chapters 5–7 and 13–14 help.
  • A VM with systemd and sudo; sudo apt install sysstat.

This chapter

Reading
about 35 minutes
Lab
25 minutes, a VM with systemd, free
Main distribution
any

At Stagedoor

Friday 13 November 2026, 19:40. It's Tiago's first week on call alone. A venue messages that its event page takes ten seconds to load; a few minutes later, two more. Nothing has alerted. Tickets for a big show go on sale at 20:00, and fans are already arriving.

Tiago has seen Rafaela do this a dozen times, and she has left him something better than memory: a script and a page in the wiki called “The first five minutes”. He logs in to door-2 and runs it.

20.1From a report to a symptom

“It's slow” isn't something you can test. Before touching a server, turn the report into a symptom you could check and later prove fixed.

  • What, exactly? Which page, API call or job; slow or failing; what error, if any.
  • For whom? Everyone, one venue, one region, mobile only? A problem for some users points at what those users share.
  • Since when? The start time is the most valuable fact you can get, because it can be matched against changes.
  • How much? Ten seconds instead of 300 milliseconds; 5% of requests failing. Measure it yourself (curl -w '%{time_total}', Chapter 14) so you can tell when it's fixed.

20.2The USE method

Brendan Gregg's USE method gives you a checklist that doesn't depend on guessing: for every resource, check its utilisation (how busy it is), saturation (how much work is waiting for it) and errors. A resource with high saturation or errors is a suspect; one that's idle with nothing waiting can be crossed off. Part III gave you the commands; here they are in one table:

Table 20.1 · USE on one Linux server
ResourceUtilisationSaturationErrors
CPU (Ch. 9)vmstat 1: us+sy; mpstat -P ALLr above the CPU count; st on VMsrare; throttling in journalctl -k
Memory (Ch. 10)free -h: availablesi/so in vmstat; /proc/pressure/memoryOOM kills in journalctl -k
Disk (Ch. 11)iostat -x: %utilaqu-sz, await; b and wa in vmstat; D statesI/O errors in journalctl -k
Space and inodes (Ch. 11)df -h, df -i(full is full)ENOSPC in app logs
Network (Ch. 13, 14)sar -n DEV 1: throughput vs link speedss -s; TcpExtListenOverflowsip -s link: errors, drops; retransmits
Limits (Ch. 12)/proc/<pid>/fd vs limitaccept queue (ss -lnt)EMFILE, EAGAIN in logs
Services (Ch. 6, 7)restarts, timers running now—systemctl --failed, journalctl -p err

Key idea

Check every resource, not the one you suspect. The resource that's saturated is often not the one the symptom points to.

20.3The first five minutes

Under pressure, people check what they checked last time. A script doesn't: it runs the whole sweep in the same order every time, changes nothing, and produces one screen you can paste into the incident channel. The lab's first5.sh is one; adapt it to your servers. Then read the output in the order of Figure 20.1:

Read first5.sh's output top to bottom, comparing each number with what you know is normal (which is why it's worth running on a calm day too, as the lab does): the load against the CPU count, vmstat's r, b, wa and si/so, available memory, space and inodes, busy disks and their queues, the busiest processes by CPU and by I/O, processes stuck in D, listen-queue overflows, failed units, recent errors, and the kernel's own complaints. Usually one or two lines stand out; the rest rule things out, which is just as useful.

20.4What changed?

Most incidents follow a change: a deploy, a configuration edit, a timer that now runs at a different time, more traffic, a dependency that changed under you. Match the symptom's start time against:

journalctl --since "19:00" --until "19:45" -p notice     # everything notable on this server in the window
systemctl list-timers --all                             # what runs on a schedule, and when it last ran
grep -h " install \| upgrade " /var/log/dpkg.log | tail   # package changes
last -n 10; sudo journalctl -u ssh --since today | grep Accepted   # who logged in
git -C ~/ops log --since "2 days ago" --oneline        # changes to the operations repository

And outside the server: the deploy history, the provider's status page, the dependencies' dashboards. “Nothing changed” is a hypothesis to check, not a fact.

20.5Act small, verify, write it down

  • Mitigate first. Stop the harm with the smallest, most reversible step: stop a job, roll back a deploy, move traffic to another server. The root cause can wait until users are fine.
  • One change at a time, each noted with its time, so you know which one worked and can undo the others.
  • Verify with the same measurement you used for the symptom: the page loads in 300 ms again, not “the load went down”.
  • Write it down while it's fresh: the timeline, what you saw, what you did, what you're not sure of. A short, blameless incident review afterwards asks how the system let it happen and what would catch it earlier, not who to blame. Every chapter's story in this book ends with exactly that kind of note.

Watch out: restarting as diagnosis

Restarting a service or rebooting a server often makes a symptom go away, and takes the evidence with it: the stuck process, the full queue, the open file. Collect the first five minutes first (it takes about twenty seconds), then restart if that's the right mitigation. And if a restart “fixed” it, the cause is still there.

20.6When it isn't this server

A server that's healthy by every USE check can still be slow for its users, because it's waiting on something else: the database, a payment provider, DNS. Signs: requests take long but the CPUs are idle, wa is low and nothing is in D; many connections sit in ESTABLISHED to one address (ss -tn). Follow the dependency: run the same sweep on the next machine, or the connection method from Chapter 14 towards it. Doing this across many services at once is what metrics, traces and dashboards are for; Handbook 7 picks up there.

20.7Across distributions

History, not just now

Every tool in this chapter exists on every distribution; sysstat has to be installed on Ubuntu, Debian and Amazon Linux. Enable its collector (sudo systemctl enable --now sysstat) and it records CPU, memory, disk and network every ten minutes, so sar -d -f /var/log/sysstat/sa13 (on RHEL, /var/log/sa/sa13) can answer “what was the disk doing at 19:40 last Friday?” after the fact. On the cloud, the provider's agent sends the same numbers to its monitoring service.

20.8Lab: the mystery slow box

Lab 20 · Be the on-call engineer

You'll run the first-five-minutes script on a calm machine, then start a hidden problem without reading how it works, find it with the script and the USE method, confirm it, and stop it. You need a VM with systemd, sudo and sudo apt install sysstat; ideally Lab 18's app running, so there's something to look at. Cost: nothing. Clean-up: sudo ./mystery.sh stop; the problem also stops by itself after ten minutes. Outputs come from a fresh systemd test container named door-2.

  1. The script. Save as ~/lab20/first5.sh and make it executable:

    first5.shbash

    #!/usr/bin/env bash
# first5.sh · the first five minutes on a slow server: one screen of facts, nothing changed
set -uo pipefail                      # no -e on purpose: one failing check mustn't stop the others

section() { printf '\n== %s\n' "$1"; }

section "load ($(nproc) CPUs)"
uptime
section "CPU, run queue, blocked, swap, I/O wait: vmstat 1 5 (skip the first line)"
vmstat 1 5
section "memory"
free -h
section "space and inodes on /"
df -h /; df -i /
section "busy disks: utilisation and latency (iostat, second report)"
iostat -dx 1 2 | awk '
  /^Device/ { n++; for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) col[$i] = i; if (n == 2) print "device  w/s  wkB/s  w_await  aqu-sz  %util"; next }
  n == 2 && NF && $col["%util"] > 0 { print $1, $col["w/s"], $col["wkB/s"], $col["w_await"], $col["aqu-sz"], $col["%util"] }'
section "top processes by CPU"
ps -eo pid,user,pcpu,pmem,stat,comm --sort=-pcpu | head -6
section "processes waiting on the disk (state D)"
ps -eo pid,user,stat,wchan:22,comm | awk 'NR == 1 || $3 ~ /D/'
section "processes doing disk I/O (pidstat, 3 seconds)"
pidstat -d 1 3 | awk '/^Average/ && ($4 + $5 > 0 || $NF == "Command")'
section "network: sockets and listen-queue overflows"
ss -s | head -2; nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows | tail -1
section "failed units"
systemctl --failed --no-legend --no-pager
section "errors in the journal, last 15 minutes"
journalctl -p err --since -15min --no-pager -q | tail -5
section "kernel: OOM kills, I/O errors, hung tasks (last hour)"
journalctl -k --since -1h --no-pager -q | grep -iE 'killed process|i/o error|blocked for more' | tail -5
    No set -e: a check that fails (a tool not installed, say) mustn't hide the others. Only reading commands: it's safe to run on any server, at any time.

  3. The mystery. Save the next script as mystery.sh without reading it (it's at the end of the lab), and start it:

  5. Confirm. Who are these processes, and who started them? 
    ps -eo pid,ppid,etime,args | grep "[t]humbs-cleanup" | cut -c1-150
        384       1       00:44 timeout 600 bash -c while :; do /var/tmp/lab20/thumbs-cleanup if=/dev/zero of=/var/tmp/lab20/.cache bs=1M count=400 oflag=
    385     384       00:44 bash -c while :; do /var/tmp/lab20/thumbs-cleanup if=/dev/zero of=/var/tmp/lab20/.cache bs=1M count=400 oflag=direct statu
    491     385       00:00 /var/tmp/lab20/thumbs-cleanup if=/dev/zero of=/var/tmp/lab20/.cache bs=1M count=400 oflag=direct status=none
    A loop (PID 385) started 44 seconds ago, under timeout, that runs thumbs-cleanup again and again, each run writing 400 MB straight to disk. Each run lives only a fraction of a second, so pidstat credits most of the I/O to the parent loop. On a real server, the next questions are “what started the loop?” (ps -o ppid up the tree, systemctl status <pid> names the unit) and “since when?” (etime, the journal).
  6. Act and verify. Stop it, then run first5.sh again and compare with calm.txt: 
    sudo ./mystery.sh stop
    stopped
    Now read the mystery:

    mystery.shbash

    #!/usr/bin/env bash
# mystery.sh start|stop · make this machine slow in one particular way. Don't read it before the lab!
set -euo pipefail
dir=/var/tmp/lab20
case "${1:-}" in
  start)
    mkdir -p "$dir"
    cp /usr/bin/dd "$dir/thumbs-cleanup"                    # a familiar-sounding name
    nohup timeout 600 bash -c "while :; do $dir/thumbs-cleanup if=/dev/zero of=$dir/.cache bs=1M count=400 oflag=direct status=none; done" >/dev/null 2>&1 &
    echo "started: something is now slowing this machine down (it stops by itself after 10 minutes)" ;;
  stop)
    pkill -f "$dir/thumbs-cleanup" || true
    pkill -f "while :; do $dir/thumbs-cleanup" || true
    rm -rf "$dir"
    echo "stopped" ;;
  *) echo "usage: sudo $0 start|stop" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
    A copy of dd under a reassuring name: a reminder that a process's name tells you what someone called it, not what it does (/proc/<pid>/exe tells you what it is).

Stretch goals. (1) Change mystery.sh to burn CPU instead (Chapter 9's burn.sh), or eat memory under a limit (Chapter 10's hog.py), and see which sections of first5.sh change. (2) Add a section for the app's own health: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n' http://127.0.0.1:8000/. (3) Enable sysstat's collector, run the mystery for ten minutes, and find it afterwards with sar -d.

At Stagedoor: 19:40 to 19:52

Tiago's output looks like the lab's: door-2's data disk at 94% utilisation, a queue of 30, I/O wait at 40%, and one find process in D, run by thumbs-cleanup.service. systemctl list-timers answers “what changed”: on Thursday, Sasha's team changed the thumbnail clean-up from Chapter 11 from nightly to hourly, to keep the cache small. With millions of files, each run's find walks the whole tree for most of the hour; at quiet times nobody noticed, and on a Friday evening, with fans browsing ahead of an on-sale, every page that needed a thumbnail waited behind it.

At 19:48 he stops the running clean-up (systemctl stop thumbs-cleanup.service, which, being a service, he can do cleanly) and checks: event pages load in 280 ms again. At 19:52 he posts his notes and the two first5.sh outputs, before and after, in the operations channel. The on-sale at 20:00 is uneventful. On Monday the timer goes back to nightly at 03:30 Lisbon time, with Nice=10 and IOSchedulingClass=idle (Chapter 9), and the app learns to delete a poster's thumbnails when the poster changes. Rafaela's only comment on his notes: add the time you started.

20.9Common mistakes

MistakeWhat happensInstead
Starting from a guessHours on the wrong resource.A USE sweep of everything, in the same order every time.
A vague symptomYou can't tell when it's fixed.What, who, since when, how much; measure it.
Skipping “what changed?”The cause sits in a deploy log nobody opened.Match the start time against changes, every time.
Restarting firstThe evidence disappears; the cause stays.Collect first (twenty seconds), then mitigate.
Several changes at onceNobody knows which one helped, or which one hurt.One change, noted with its time, then verify.
No baselineEvery number looks suspicious, or none does.Run the checks on a calm day; keep history (sysstat).
No notesThe same incident, solved from scratch next time.A short, blameless write-up with the timeline.

✓Chapter summary

  • Turn reports into a precise symptom: what, for whom, since when, how much.
  • The USE method checks utilisation, saturation and errors for every resource, so you don't depend on a hunch.
  • A first-five-minutes script runs the whole sweep, read-only, the same way every time; compare it with a calm baseline.
  • Ask what changed; confirm a candidate before acting; mitigate with the smallest safe step; verify with the original measurement.
  • Write it down, blamelessly. If this server is healthy, follow the dependency.

Key terms

USE method
A troubleshooting checklist: for every resource, check utilisation, saturation and errors.
Utilisation
The proportion of time, or of capacity, a resource is busy.
Saturation
The amount of work waiting for a resource because it's busy, such as a run queue or a disk queue.
Mitigation
An action that stops or reduces an incident's harm, separate from fixing its root cause.
Baseline (performance)
The normal values of a system's measurements, recorded when it's healthy, for comparison during incidents.
Blameless review
A write-up after an incident that examines how the system allowed it, not who to blame.

Check your understanding

  1. Give the utilisation, saturation and errors checks for memory. recall

    Show answer

    Utilisation: free -h, mainly available. Saturation: swapping (si/so in vmstat 1) and memory pressure (/proc/pressure/memory). Errors: OOM kills in journalctl -k or dmesg.

  2. A venue says “checkout is broken”. Write four questions that turn this into a symptom you can test. apply

    Show answer

    What exactly happens: an error message, a spinner, a wrong total? For which events, devices, payment methods? Since when, and is it every time or sometimes? Can you reproduce it, and how long does it take (time a request yourself with curl)? Also: is it only that venue?

  3. Explain why a script that changes nothing is preferable to a person typing commands during an incident. explain

    Show answer

    Under pressure, people skip steps and check what they suspect. A script checks everything, in the same order, in seconds, produces output that can be compared with a baseline and shared, and can't make things worse because it only reads. It also lets less experienced people do a thorough first look.

  4. first5.sh shows idle CPUs, low I/O wait, nothing in D, free memory and space, but users still wait ten seconds per request. What do you look at next? debug

    Show answer

    The server is probably waiting on something else. Look at where its requests go: ss -tnp for many connections to one address (a database, an API), the app's logs for slow downstream calls, then the dependency itself, with the same sweep or the connection method from Chapter 14. Also check limits that don't show as resource use: connection pools, accept queues, worker counts.

  5. Design the “first five minutes” page for Stagedoor's wiki. design

    Show answer

    Step 0: write the symptom and its start time in the incident channel. Step 1: run first5.sh on the affected server(s) and paste the output, next to the latest calm baseline. Step 2: check what changed: deploys, timers, config commits, the provider's status. Step 3: USE reading guide (which lines matter and what's normal for each server). Step 4: common mitigations with their commands (stop a job, roll back, take a server out of the load balancer). Step 5: notes template. Plus who to call, and when.

  6. Compare mitigating by restarting the app with mitigating by stopping the job that's saturating the disk. compare

    Show answer

    Restarting the app might briefly help, interrupts users and in-flight requests, destroys evidence and leaves the cause (the job) running, so the symptom returns. Stopping the job addresses the confirmed cause directly, is reversible (it can run again later) and keeps the app's state. Mitigate at the cause you've confirmed.

Going further

  • Google SRE book, chapter Effective Troubleshooting and Postmortem Culture.
  • man sar, man iostat, man pidstat.

Part VI · Running it

21

Capstone: Stagedoor's servers end to end

In January, Stagedoor had three servers that nobody could describe. This chapter puts the whole book to work: a web server built from a written baseline by one idempotent script, checked for drift, then put through an on-sale drill until it holds. It ends where a cloud migration can begin: with servers you could rebuild tomorrow.

By the end you can

  • Turn a server baseline into a build script that's idempotent and has a check mode.
  • Build a web server from nothing with it, and detect and repair drift.
  • Run a load drill and a crash drill, and read what they tell you.
  • Deploy a fix as a new release through the same script.
  • Hand a server over with a short, honest list of what isn't covered yet.

Before you start

  • The whole book, especially 6, 12, 15–18 and 20.
  • A fresh Ubuntu 24.04 VM with systemd and sudo that you can throw away, and sudo apt install apache2-utils for ab.

This chapter

Reading
about 40 minutes
Lab
60 minutes, a disposable VM, free
Main distribution
Ubuntu 24.04

At Stagedoor

door-2 runs Ubuntu 22.04, whose standard support ends in April 2027, and it has been fixed by hand, carefully, twelve times this year. On Thursday 19 November 2026, Rafaela and Tiago build its replacement, door-5, at Atlantica Hosting: a new Ubuntu 24.04 VM, nothing on it but what the build script puts there. On Tuesday 24 November, before anyone sends it a real fan, they run an on-sale drill against it.

Joana's question from July (Chapter 12) is the goal: how would we know before an on-sale? The answer is this chapter.

21.1The year in one table

Every problem in this book left a rule behind. Together, they're the baseline the build script encodes:

Table 21.1 · Stagedoor's 2026, and what each incident added to the baseline
Ch.What happenedWhat the baseline now says
1three undocumented servers, a root password in the chatevery server described in writing
3, 4app in /root, uploads 777FHS layout, own user, 2750 + UMask=0027, personal accounts and sudo
5, 6kill -9 deploys; a cron job broken by PATHsystemd service with graceful stop; timers with full paths

8updates off for ten monthsdaily security updates, weekly restart window

15, 16everything reachable; Marco's keynftables default deny; SSH keys only, no root, AllowGroups
17, 18a clean-up script deleted uploads; findingsstrict mode and ShellCheck; sandboxed units; a written baseline
19, 2010-second container stops; an hourly findexec-form entrypoints with an init; the first five minutes

21.2From baseline to server

The script follows one pattern for every item: a check function that answers “is this item as the baseline says?” and a fix function that makes it so. The script runs the check; if it fails, it runs the fix and the check again, and stops if it still fails. That gives three properties for free:

  • Idempotent (Chapter 17): a second run finds every item ok and changes nothing, so it's always safe to run again, including after a half-finished first run.
  • A check mode: with --check, it reports what differs and changes nothing. Run on a schedule, that's drift detection: a hand edit or a stray package shows up the next morning.
  • Small, visible changes: each line of output says whether that item was already right or was fixed.

This is exactly what configuration-management tools such as Ansible do, with a library of ready-made, tested “check and fix” modules and many machines at once. The book's script is the same idea at a size you can read in one sitting; Stagedoor will move to Ansible or to images built by CI when it moves to the cloud (Handbook 5).

Key idea

A server you can rebuild from a script in minutes is a server you can test, replace, scale and trust. A server you can only repair is a pet.

21.3What writing the script taught

The script below was tested on a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 system, and the testing found four bugs in its first drafts, each one a lesson from an earlier chapter turning up again:

  1. set -e is off inside if (Chapter 17). The checks run inside a test, so a check with several commands reported success whenever its last command succeeded. Every check now joins its tests with && or || return 1.
  2. grep -q plus pipefail (Chapter 2). sshd -T | grep -q … failed although the line was there: grep -q exits at the first match, sshd dies writing to the closed pipe (SIGPIPE), and pipefail reports that as a failure. After a long-output command, use grep … >/dev/null.
  3. A new release isn't running until the service restarts (Chapter 5, Chapter 8). The first draft switched current to the new release and reported success while the old code kept running. The fix restarts the service when its release changes.
  4. sshd -t needs /run/sshd, which Ubuntu 24.04 creates only when ssh.socket first starts sshd. On a fresh server nobody has connected to yet, the check failed with “Missing privilege separation directory”. The script creates it.

None of these would have been found by reading. All four were found by running the script on a machine built for the purpose and throwing it away afterwards, which is the habit this chapter is really about.

21.4Drills

A server that builds cleanly can still fail under load, and the only way to know is to load it. Two drills cover most of what goes wrong on an on-sale:

  • A load drill. More concurrent requests than the busiest real moment, through the same path as real traffic (nginx in front of the app), while you watch everything Chapter 20 taught: first5.sh, nginx's error and access logs, listen-queue overflows. ab (Apache Bench) is enough to start; hey, wrk, k6 and Locust do more realistic traffic.
  • A failure drill. Kill something on purpose during the load (the app, a whole server), and measure what users see and how long recovery takes. It tests restart policies, health checks and whether there's a second server to take over.

Run drills against a copy, never against the servers fans are using; announce them; stop at the first sign of harm to anything real; and write down the numbers, because the next drill compares with them.

21.5Handover: what isn't covered yet

A build script is never the whole story, and pretending it is would be the most dangerous line in the runbook. An honest handover lists what the script doesn't do, with who owns each item:

Table 21.2 · Not in the build script yet, for door-5
ItemWhere it stands
auditd rules (Chapter 18)applied by hand, to be added
Log and audit shipping (Chapter 7, 16)agent installed by hand; config in Git, not in the script
TLS certificates (Chapter 14)certbot on door-3 distributes to the web servers
Monitoring and alerts (Chapters 9–12)agent and alert rules managed separately
Uploads sync and backups (Chapter 4, 17)timers to be moved into the script
The data volume (Chapter 11)attached and mounted by hand at Atlantica

The list shrinks with each release of the script, and it's the first thing to read before relying on a rebuild.

21.6Lab: build door-5, then try to break it

Lab 21 · The capstone

You'll assemble the baseline from earlier chapters' files, build a web server from nothing, show it's idempotent, introduce drift and watch the check catch it, run a load drill that fails, fix the cause as a new release, drill again, and kill the app under load. You need a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 VM with systemd that you'll throw away afterwards (it changes SSH, the firewall and nginx), sudo, and sudo apt install apache2-utils. Before running the script, make sure the firewall's SSH rule allows your address, or work from the VM's console. Cost: nothing. Clean-up: delete the VM. Outputs come from a fresh systemd test container named door-5, run as root.

  1. The baseline directory. Create ~/build with three things. The script:

    build-web.shbash

    #!/usr/bin/env bash
# build-web.sh [--check] · build a Stagedoor web server from the baseline, or check one against it.
# Run as root from the directory holding files/ and keys/. Safe to run again: it fixes only what differs.
set -euo pipefail
cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")"

mode=build; [[ ${1:-} == --check ]] && mode=check
release=${RELEASE:-2026.11.1}
problems=0

# ensure "description" CHECK FIX: run CHECK; if it fails, run FIX and CHECK again (or, in --check mode, report it).
# CHECK functions run inside "if", where set -e is off (Chapter 17), so each one joins its tests with && or "|| return 1".
# After a long-output command, use "grep … >/dev/null", not "grep -q": -q exits early, the writer dies of SIGPIPE,
# and pipefail turns that into a failure.
ensure() {
  local what=$1 check=$2 fix=$3
  printf '%-50s ' "$what"
  if "$check" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "ok"; return; fi
  if [[ $mode == check ]]; then echo "DIFFERS"; problems=$((problems + 1)); return; fi
  "$fix" >/dev/null
  if "$check" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "fixed"; else echo "FAILED"; exit 1; fi
}
same() { cmp -s "files/$1" "$2"; }                    # is the installed file exactly our copy?
put()  { install -D -m "${3:-644}" "files/$1" "$2"; }  # install our copy

# 1. packages (Chapter 8)
pkgs=(nginx nftables openssh-server unattended-upgrades needrestart python3)
c_pkgs() { for p in "${pkgs[@]}"; do dpkg-query -W -f='${Status}' "$p" | grep -q "install ok installed" || return 1; done; }
f_pkgs() { apt-get update -q && DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y -q "${pkgs[@]}"; }
ensure "packages installed" c_pkgs f_pkgs

# 2. people: personal accounts in sudo and ssh-users, password locked, key from keys/ (Chapters 4, 16)
c_people() {
  getent group ssh-users || return 1
  for k in keys/*.pub; do
    u=$(basename "$k" .pub)
    id -nG "$u" | grep -qw ssh-users && id -nG "$u" | grep -qw sudo &&
      cmp -s "$k" "/home/$u/.ssh/authorized_keys" || return 1
  done
}
f_people() {
  getent group ssh-users || groupadd ssh-users
  for k in keys/*.pub; do
    u=$(basename "$k" .pub)
    id "$u" >/dev/null 2>&1 || useradd --create-home --shell /bin/bash "$u"
    usermod -aG sudo,ssh-users "$u"; passwd -l "$u"
    install -d -o "$u" -g "$u" -m 700 "/home/$u/.ssh"
    install -o "$u" -g "$u" -m 600 "$k" "/home/$u/.ssh/authorized_keys"
  done
}
ensure "people and their SSH keys" c_people f_people

# 3. SSH: keys only, no root, ssh-users only (Chapter 16). sshd -t and -T need /run/sshd, which Ubuntu 24.04
#    creates only when ssh.socket first starts sshd, so make sure it exists.
c_ssh() { install -d -m 755 /run/sshd && same sshd.conf /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-stagedoor.conf && sshd -T | grep -x "permitrootlogin no" >/dev/null; }
f_ssh() { put sshd.conf /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-stagedoor.conf; sshd -t; systemctl try-reload-or-restart ssh; }
ensure "sshd hardened" c_ssh f_ssh

# 4. the app: user, release layout, config, data (Chapters 3, 4, 6)
c_app_files() {
  id stagedoor &&
  same app.py "/opt/stagedoor/releases/$release/app.py" &&
  [[ $(readlink /opt/stagedoor/current) == "releases/$release" ]] &&
  same stagedoor.env /etc/stagedoor/stagedoor.env &&
  [[ $(stat -c '%U:%G %a' /etc/stagedoor/stagedoor.env) == "root:stagedoor 640" ]] &&
  [[ $(stat -c '%U:%G %a' /var/lib/stagedoor) == "stagedoor:stagedoor 750" ]]
}
f_app_files() {
  id stagedoor >/dev/null 2>&1 || useradd --system --user-group --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin stagedoor
  put app.py "/opt/stagedoor/releases/$release/app.py"
  ln -s "releases/$release" /opt/stagedoor/current.new && mv -T /opt/stagedoor/current.new /opt/stagedoor/current
  install -d -o root -g stagedoor -m 750 /etc/stagedoor
  install -o root -g stagedoor -m 640 files/stagedoor.env /etc/stagedoor/stagedoor.env
  install -d -o stagedoor -g stagedoor -m 750 /var/lib/stagedoor
  if systemctl is-active -q stagedoor; then systemctl restart stagedoor; fi   # new code runs only after a restart
}
ensure "app release $release, config and data" c_app_files f_app_files

# 5. the app as a sandboxed service (Chapters 6, 12, 18)
c_app_unit() {
  same stagedoor.service /etc/systemd/system/stagedoor.service &&
  same hardening.conf /etc/systemd/system/stagedoor.service.d/hardening.conf &&
  systemctl is-enabled stagedoor && systemctl is-active stagedoor
}
f_app_unit() {
  put stagedoor.service /etc/systemd/system/stagedoor.service
  put hardening.conf /etc/systemd/system/stagedoor.service.d/hardening.conf
  systemctl daemon-reload; systemctl enable -q stagedoor; systemctl restart stagedoor; sleep 1
}
ensure "stagedoor.service enabled and running" c_app_unit f_app_unit

# 6. nginx in front, with limits for on-sales (Chapters 12, 14)
c_nginx() {
  same nginx-site.conf /etc/nginx/sites-available/stagedoor &&
  [[ $(readlink /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/stagedoor) == /etc/nginx/sites-available/stagedoor ]] &&
  [[ ! -e /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default ]] &&
  grep -q "worker_rlimit_nofile 65536;" /etc/nginx/nginx.conf &&
  grep -q "worker_connections 8192;" /etc/nginx/nginx.conf &&
  same nginx-limits.conf /etc/systemd/system/nginx.service.d/limits.conf &&
  nginx -tq && systemctl is-active nginx
}
f_nginx() {
  put nginx-site.conf /etc/nginx/sites-available/stagedoor
  ln -sfn /etc/nginx/sites-available/stagedoor /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/stagedoor
  rm -f /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default
  grep -q "worker_rlimit_nofile" /etc/nginx/nginx.conf || sed -i "s/^worker_processes auto;/&\nworker_rlimit_nofile 65536;/" /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
  sed -i "s/worker_connections [0-9]*;/worker_connections 8192;/" /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
  put nginx-limits.conf /etc/systemd/system/nginx.service.d/limits.conf
  nginx -tq; systemctl daemon-reload; systemctl restart nginx
}
ensure "nginx site, limits and backlog" c_nginx f_nginx

# 7. host firewall (Chapter 15)
c_fw() { same web.nft /etc/nftables.conf && systemctl is-enabled nftables && nft list chain inet filter input | grep "policy drop" >/dev/null; }
f_fw() { nft -c -f files/web.nft; put web.nft /etc/nftables.conf 755; systemctl enable -q nftables; nft -f /etc/nftables.conf; }
ensure "nftables default deny" c_fw f_fw

# 8. logs, kernel settings, updates (Chapters 7, 8, 12, 18)
c_misc() {
  same journald.conf /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/size.conf &&
  same sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/60-stagedoor.conf &&
  same auto-upgrades.conf /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/52stagedoor &&
  same needrestart.conf /etc/needrestart/conf.d/50-stagedoor.conf
}
f_misc() {
  put journald.conf /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/size.conf; systemctl restart systemd-journald
  put sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/60-stagedoor.conf; sysctl -q -p /etc/sysctl.d/60-stagedoor.conf
  put auto-upgrades.conf /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/52stagedoor
  put needrestart.conf /etc/needrestart/conf.d/50-stagedoor.conf
}
ensure "journald, sysctl, updates, needrestart" c_misc f_misc

# 9. the end-to-end check: a request through nginx reaches the app
c_http() { curl -sf http://127.0.0.1/ | grep -q "as stagedoor"; }
f_http() { false; }
ensure "http://127.0.0.1/ answered by the app" c_http f_http

if (( problems )); then echo "$problems item(s) differ from the baseline"; exit 1; fi
echo "server matches the baseline"
    A keys/ directory with one public key per person, named after them (keys/rafaela.pub, keys/tiago.pub: use your own). And a files/ directory. Two of its files are new:

    files/nginx-site.confnginx

    # /etc/nginx/sites-available/stagedoor · the public site, proxied to the app
upstream stagedoor_app {
    server 127.0.0.1:8000;
    keepalive 32;                                   # reuse connections to the app (Chapter 12)
}

server {
    listen 80 default_server backlog=4096;          # a long accept queue for on-sales (Chapter 12)
    server_name tickets.stagedoor.example;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://stagedoor_app;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_read_timeout 30s;
    }
}

    files/web.nftnftables

# /etc/nftables.conf · web server: HTTP from anywhere, SSH from the office VPN only (Chapter 15)
flush ruleset

table inet filter {
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority filter; policy drop;

        ct state established,related accept
        ct state invalid drop
        iif "lo" accept
        ip protocol icmp accept

        tcp dport { 80, 443 } accept comment "the public site"
        tcp dport 22 ip saddr 198.51.100.20 accept comment "SSH from the office VPN"

        counter comment "everything else is dropped"
    }
}

  6. Load drill. 20,000 requests, 200 at a time, through nginx; then why the failures: 
    sudo nstat -n
ab -q -n 20000 -c 200 http://127.0.0.1/ 2>&1 | grep -E "^(Complete requests|Failed requests|Non-2xx|Requests per second|Time per request:.*mean\)|  99%)"

Time per request:       320.622 [ms] (mean)
  99%   2043
    sudo awk '$9 != 200 {print $9}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c
nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows | tail -1; ss -lnt "sport = :8000"
        143 504
TcpExtListenOverflows           2431               0.0
State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:PortProcess
LISTEN 0      5          127.0.0.1:8000      0.0.0.0:*
    143 requests timed out at nginx (504), the slowest 1% took two seconds, and the app's accept queue overflowed thousands of times: its listen backlog (Send-Q) is 5. Python's http.server asks for 5 by default, exactly Chapter 12's trap: nginx's limits were raised, the app's weren't.
  7. Fix it as a release. Add one line to files/app.py, just before the server is created: 
    http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer.request_queue_size = 1024   # listen backlog; Python's default is 5 (Chapter 12)
    change STAGEDOOR_VERSION in files/stagedoor.env to 2026.11.2, and deploy with the same script: 
    sudo RELEASE=2026.11.2 ./build-web.sh | grep -v " ok$"
ls /opt/stagedoor/releases; readlink /opt/stagedoor/current; ss -lnt "sport = :8000"

server matches the baseline
